judge_assessment.explanation: The hard failure is exact, and I checked it in the source rather than the rendered page. worksheet.tex problem 4 prints two response slots -- 'Write 18 as a number word: \underline{\hspace{4cm}}' and 'is one ten and \ansblank ones' -- while verify.json id 4 is a single eval (18-10 -> 8) covering the digit only; problem 6 has the identical two-slot structure for 'twelve' against a single eval (12-10 -> 2); and problem 10 instructs 'First write each number word as a numeral' before the comparison, while verify.json id 10 records only the relation. Three number-word or numeral responses are objectively checkable (a teen number word is a closed vocabulary the worksheet even prints in its directions) and none is in the verification data, while final_response.md claims 'the per-problem binding that ties every printed boxed answer back to its verified value'. The mathematics is right: 13, 17, 14, eighteen/8, 19, twelve/2, 16, 5, <, and 14 < 17, matching both the key and my own recomputation. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 4 and 6 teach the right thing in the right way: instead of letting the child read the ones off the second digit, the key derives them by subtracting the ten (18 - 10 = 8, 12 - 10 = 2). That is the actual place-value move, and it is what makes 'the 1 means one ten' stick.

Twelve is deliberately paired with eighteen. The key says so explicitly -- 'Twelve is a name that must be memorised --- it does not say "two-teen" --- but its place value works the same way' -- which separates the irregular spoken name from the regular place-value structure.

Problem 8 (Rosa's 15 stickers, one ten bagged) carries a declared trap for reading the leading 1 as one one, giving 14. That is the single most common teen-number error and it is machine-checked as distinguishable.

Four distinct problem skeletons -- ten-frame to numeral, ten-and-ones to numeral, word to numeral, numeral to word plus place-value sentence, then comparison -- so the no-repeated-skeleton requirement is genuinely met.

root_causes.description: The coverage contract is stated per PROBLEM, not per printed RESPONSE SLOT. SKILL.md's JSON-format section says verification 'hard-fails unless every problem id 1..N has at least one check', and verify.py enforces exactly that. One check therefore discharges a problem that prints two or three separate things for the student to write, and the gate chain reports the sheet as fully verified.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 4: '\par Write 18 as a number word: \underline{\hspace{4cm}}' AND '18 is one ten and \ansblank ones' -- two printed slots; verify.json id 4 is one eval (18-10 -> 8), covering the digit only
worksheet.tex problem 6: identical structure for 'twelve'; verify.json id 6 is one eval (12-10 -> 2)
worksheet problem 10: 'First write each number word as a numeral. Then write < or >' -- verify.json id 10 is a lone compare of 14 vs 17; the numerals 14 and 17 are unrecorded
SKILL.md: 'every problem id 1..N has at least one check'

root_causes.description: The Quick Answers bank blanks the two verified relations for the same sympify reason seen across this run, so the grading column silently under-reports what was verified.

Problem 10 prints ONE blank ('Sam's number \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}} Mia's number') but issues three instructions: write 14, write 17, and write the relation. A child can reasonably write '14' in the only blank available. Separately, the study guide's Skill 2 rule announces 'the three that hide their pattern' and then lists four (eleven, twelve, thirteen, fifteen).
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 10, single \underline slot after a three-part instruction
study_guide.pdf Skill 2: 'Learn the three that hide their pattern: eleven, twelve, and thirteen (three), fifteen (five).'

improvements.title: Every printed response slot needs its own verification entry, not one per problem
improvements.proposed_change: Change the coverage rule from 'one check per problem id' to 'one check per printed response slot'. Concretely: (a) rewrite the SKILL.md JSON-format sentence to require an entry for every blank, box or \ansblank the item prints, using a `manual` entry when a slot is a mark or a sentence; (b) have tests/check_layout.py count the response macros inside each \problem segment and fail when that count exceeds the number of verify entries carrying that id. The schema already supports several entries per id -- Problems 4 and 6 each need a second entry for the number word. A closed vocabulary like the teen words can be checked exactly (an expected-string entry), so these do not have to be manual.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture worksheet whose problem 1 prints two \ansblank slots with a verify JSON carrying a single entry for id 1, and assert check_layout.py exits non-zero naming problem 1. It passes (exit 0) today, which is the defect.
improvements.expected_impact: Restores coverage of the responses the prompt names first -- 'reading and writing teen numerals and number words'. Today the number words, which are the topic, are the only printed answers not bound.
improvements.risk: Medium. Counting response macros will initially fire on sheets that print a decorative underline, and on the 'Answer:' line that some templates emit in addition to an inline blank. Land the checker in warn-only mode for one run, tune against the existing eval corpus, then make it a hard gate.

improvements.title: Quick Answers bank prints an em-dash instead of the verified > / < relation
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, _fmt() sends every string 'expected' through sympy.sympify(); '>' and '<' raise SympifyError and fall through to the '---' branch, which the module's own docstring reserves for 'see solution' / manual-only ids. Add a relation branch before the sympify attempt: map the bare relation tokens ('>', '<', '>=', '<=', '=', '≥', '≤') to their math-mode LaTeX ($>$, $<$, $\ge$, $\le$, $=$) and return that. Everything else keeps its current behaviour, so genuinely manual ids still print '---' and remain distinguishable from a verified relation.
improvements.regression_test: Add a case to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py that renders a verify JSON containing {"id": 1, "type": "compare", "values": ["5+3", "4+2"], "order": "relation", "expected": ">"} alongside a {"id": 2, "type": "manual"} entry, and asserts the bank line for id 1 contains '$>$' while the line for id 2 is '---'. It fails today because both render '---'.
improvements.expected_impact: Every worksheet whose verification_targets include 'compare' with order 'relation' regains real entries in the grader's at-a-glance bank. In this shard alone that is curr-002 (2 of 10 entries), curr-006 (2 of 8), curr-032 (2 of 10), curr-038 (part of entry 8) and curr-050 (2 of 10).
improvements.risk: Low and contained to the bank. The entries are plain text by design and are never read by check_answer_key.py, so the strict per-problem binding gate cannot be affected. Only risk is choosing a LaTeX spelling that does not compile, which the existing compile-ak gate would catch immediately.

improvements.title: Problem 10 asks for three responses and prints one blank
improvements.proposed_change: Rewrite problem 10 in worksheet.tex so each requested response has its own slot: 'Sam: fourteen = \ansblank    Mia: seventeen = \ansblank' on one line, then 'Sam's number \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}} Mia's number' underneath. Then declare three verify entries under id 10 (14, 17, and the relation). Generalise via the same response-slot counter proposed under verify-every-printed-answer-slot, which catches the mismatch in the other direction as well.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem whose prose contains three imperative 'write' clauses but only one response macro; assert check_layout.py reports the instruction/slot mismatch. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: A child following the instructions has somewhere to put each answer, and the ambiguity of writing '14' into the comparison blank disappears.
improvements.risk: Low; layout-only change to one problem plus one lint.

improvements.title: Study guide says 'the three that hide their pattern' then lists four
improvements.proposed_change: Fix the Skill 2 rule line in study_guide.tex to read 'Learn the four that hide their pattern: eleven, twelve, thirteen (three) and fifteen (five).' A cheap general guard: extend tests/check_prose_consistency.py with a number-word/list-length check that fires when a spelled-out count immediately precedes a comma-separated list of a different length.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture prose 'the three that hide their pattern: a, b, c, d' -- assert check_prose_consistency.py flags the count/list mismatch. No such check exists today.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a plainly wrong statement from instructional text a five-year-old is meant to read with an adult.
improvements.risk: Low, but the lint needs a tight pattern or it will fire on prose like 'the three steps below: read, count, write, then check'.

case_summary: The teen-number mathematics, the four-skeleton problem design and the answer key's place-value reasoning are all good, and every principal answer recomputes (13, 17, 14, 8/eighteen, 19, 2/twelve, 16, 5, <, <). The rejection is the shard's dominant defect in its purest form: problems 4 and 6 each print a number-word slot and a ones-digit slot while verification records only the digit, and problem 10 asks for two numerals before the relation and records only the relation. Three further issues the judge did not raise: the Quick Answers bank blanks both verified relations, problem 10 offers a single blank for a three-part instruction, and the study guide's Skill 2 rule says 'the three' and then lists four irregular words.
